MINUTES
  Regular Meeting
  ALHAMBRA CITY COUNCIL
  Council Chambers, 111 South First Street
  May 11, 2026
  6:00 p.m.

ROLL CALL: At 6:09 p.m., on Monday, May 11, 2026, the Alhambra City Council met in the
Council Chambers of Alhambra City Hall.

PRESENT:  LEE, MAZA, WANG, ANDRADE-STADLER, MALONEY
ABSENT:  NONE

Officials Present: City Manager Binnquist, Assistant City Manager Garcia, City Attorney Montes,
Assistant City Clerk Lamb McCarthy, Director of Parks and Recreation Macias, Director of
Finance Lieu, Director of Community Development Ho, Associate Planner Vargas, Director of
Public Works and Utilities Ahlen, Chief of Fire Department Ragusa, Chief of Police Kennedy,
Director of Library Services LohGuan, Director of Human Resources Ko, Management Analyst
Alvarez

FLAG SALUTE:  Led by Mayor Maloney

LAND ACKNOWLEDGEMENT: We acknowledge that the land on which we are gathered is the
traditional, ancestral, and unceded territory of the Gabrielino/Tongva peoples. We seek to
prioritize respect for the historic culture and contemporary presence of the native peoples
throughout California, especially in the greater Los Angeles/Alhambra area. We come with
respect and gratitude for the Gabrielino/Tongva people who still consider themselves the
caretakers of this land. It is through their examples that we are reminded of our greater
responsibility to take care of Mother Earth and to take care of each other.

CEREMONIAL

PUBLIC HEARING

2.  PUBLIC HEARING TO ADOPT ORDINANCE O2M26-4863 APPROVING ZONING TEXT
  AMENDMENT AMD-26-04 MAKING GENERAL CLARIFYING UPDATES TO THE
  CITY’S ZONING CODE; AND DETERMINE THIS ACTION IS EXEMPT FROM CEQA –
  F2M20-24, N2M26-46, O2M26-4863

  Associate Planner VARGAS presented Notice No. N2M26-46 for the City Council to hold
  a public hearing to consider an ordinance approving a Zoning Text Amendment amending
  various sections of Title 23 (Zoning) of the Alhambra Municipal Code, as well as adding
  new sections, to address new State legislation, eliminate inconsistencies, clarify
  ambiguous provisions, correct typographical and formatting errors, and modify use
  allowances. This is a City-initiated application. From time-to-time updates are made to the
  Alhambra Municipal Code (AMC) to address new State legislation, clarify ambiguous
  provisions, or delete outdated language. While some of these changes require immediate
  consideration by the Council, most can be addressed periodically. Accordingly, staff brings
  a code clean-up ordinance to the Council on an annual basis to address modifications
  needed due to new legislation, as well as other suggested clarifying changes. Clean-ups
  to the Zoning Code are processed separately from clean-ups to the rest of the AMC as
  Planning Commission review is required for Zoning and General Plan Amendments.
  Similar to prior clean-ups, this update would address new State legislation, eliminate
  inconsistencies, and create greater clarity in implementing the Zoning Code. This Zoning
  Code clean-up included both proposed amendments and additions. Amendments
  consisted of revisions to existing sections of the AMC, while additions incorporated entirely
  new sections into the AMC. The nature of and reasoning for each proposed amendment
  and addition could be classified by five (5) general categories: 1.) Clarification; 2.)
  Consistency; 3.) Compliance with State laws/Federal laws; 4.) Typographical &
  Formatting; and 5.) Use Allowances & Regulations. Some of the proposed amendments
  and additions were a combination of these five categories. In Attachment 1 of the staff
  2
5-11-26
   report for this item, each proposed amendment/addition was briefly described in a table,
  which included a breakdown of the categories applicable to each amendment/addition. All
  of the proposed amendments and additions were reviewed for consistency with the City’s
  General Plan, as required by AMC Section 23.40.080 (General Plan Consistency
  Required for Zoning Amendments).

  At their April 6, 2026 regular meeting, the Planning Commission reviewed the proposed
  amendments and additions in Ordinance No. O2M26-4863, and adopted Planning
  Commission Resolution No. 26-02 by a vote of 7-0, recommending the City Council
  approve Zoning Text Amendment AMD-26-04, with one minor revision to verbiage for
  tandem parking standards (incorporated at the recommendation of staff) and a request to
  verify accuracy of language included in two sections pertaining to Urban Dwelling Units
  (SB 9 Units). The recommendations by the Planning Commission were listed in Planning
  Commission Resolution No. 26-02, which was Attachment 3 of the staff report for this item,
  and appropriate revisions were incorporated into Ordinance No. O2M26-4863.

  The City reviewed the environmental impacts of this Ordinance under the California
  Environmental Quality Act (Public Resources Code §§ 21000, et seq. “CEQA”) and the
  regulations promulgated thereunder (14 Cal. Code of Regs. §§ 15000, et seq., the “CEQA
  Guidelines”). This Ordinance was not subject to further review environmental review
  because: (1) it would not result in a direct or reasonably foreseeable indirect physical
  change in the environment (14 Cal. Code Regs. § 15060(c)(2); (2) there was no possibility
  that this Ordinance would have a significant effect on the environment (14 Cal. Code Regs.
  § 15061(b)(3)); and (3) the Ordinance, by itself, does not constitute a “project” as defined
  in section 21065 of the Public Resources Code and the CEQA Guidelines (14 Cal. Code
  Regs. § 15378). It could be seen with certainty that there was no possibility that this
  Ordinance would have a significant effect on the environment.

  Open Public Hearing:  Mayor Maloney opened the public hearing.

  Public Comment:

  1) Brian Maida expressed concerns regarding the recent zoning amendments, noting that
  the smoke shop would cease operations due to the new zoning requirements,
  highlighting businesses were not involved early in the decision-making process and
  urged the City Council to reconsider these standards.

  2) Sara Durghalli raised objections to the vape and smoke shop regulations, due to the
  insufficient public noticing timelines and the additional requirements on the current
  business.

  3) Scott Abdulhai concerned on impact of current businesses and transparency of the
  noticing to businesses.

  4) Lewis McCammon commented that AB130, noting his understanding on state
  mandated laws but recommended that public hearings remain accessible to ensure
  transparency and community involvement.

  Close Public Hearing:  After receiving public comment, Mayor Maloney closed the
  public hearing.

  3
5-11-26
   Discussion:  Vice Mayor Andrade-Stadler received clarification on the three-year
  period to implement the proposed changes.

  Councilmember WANG supported implementing restrictions on data centers and
  emphasized the buffer requirement for vape and smoke shops, mandating that these
  businesses be spaced at least 600 feet apart, with a minimum separation of 1,000 feet to
  maintain distinction between them. She recommended that applications for Conditional
  Use Permits be processed within three years to ensure compliance for continued
  operation. Businesses that fail to meet the distance requirements after this period should
  be subject to closure.

  Councilmember LEE spoke in opposition of allowing vape and smoke shops within the
  City, and urged for the City Council to include grocery stores and other retail outlets within
  this requirement to limit the amount of buffer areas available for additional business to
  come in.

  Council Member MAZA expressed opposition to the proposed requirement requiring
  relocation of vape and smoke shops within three years and discussed the new regulations,
  emphasizing that they should not adversely affect current vape and smoke shops if there
  are no performance concerns. The proposal aims to ensure that businesses continue to
  operate in accordance with established performance standards.

  Mayor MALONEY spoke on the proposal to utilize a Director’s hearing, which aims to
  increase efficiency of approval timelines, as the director is able to hold more hearings over
  the Planning Commission meetings that are held twice a month. The directors hearing
  would still require proper noticing of the affect residence and news paper posting
  requirements. He wasn't aware that some smoke shops may need to close and is
  concerned about the current 5 businesses operating under existing regulations.

  Vice Mayor ANDRADE-STADLER proposed reviewing a performance report on the
  current businesses to help identify a balance approach that support existing
  establishments.

  Mayor MALONEY noted that if the City Council's goal is to prohibit smoke and vape shops,
  it should be reflected in the ordinances rather than focusing on increasing buffer zones or
  adding additional businesses within the designated areas.

  City Attorney Villegas clarified the City Council could: Businesses that are in compliance
  will be grandfathered and required to go through the CUP process, thus becoming legally
  non-conforming uses. If any businesses were cited, they should be addressed
  accordingly.

  Action Taken:  City Council took the following actions:

  1) Directed the City Attorney to introduce and give first reading by title, only waiving
  further reading to Ordinance entitled:

  Ordinance No. O2M26-4863: An Ordinance of the City Council of the City of
  Alhambra adopting Zoning Text Amendment AMD-26-04, amending the Alhambra
  Municipal Code to address new state laws, eliminate inconsistencies, clarify
  ambiguous provisions, correct typographical and formatting errors, and modify use
  4
5-11-26
   allowances

  with the amendment for Smoke and Vape provisions, allowing existing businesses to
  operate under a CUP, to be obtained within a three years period and subject to a compliant
  performance review, and removing buffer restrictions. Additionally, no longer permitting
  smoke and vape retail shops in Alhambra.

  which ordinance shall return for a second reading and adoption at the next City Council
  meeting on June 22, 2026; and,

  2) Determined the action was exempt from CEQA.

  Vote:  Moved:  LEE  Seconded: MAZA
  Ayes:  MAZA, LEE, WANG, MALONEY, ANDRADE-STADLER
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

3.  PUBLIC WORKS MAINTENANCE & IMPROVEMENT DISTRICT FISCAL YEAR 2026-
  2027 RENEWAL – F2M26-28, N2M26-51, R2M26-13

  Director of Public Works and Utilities AHLEN delivered a staff report. This was the time
  and place set by Notice No. N2M26-51 for the City Council to hold a public hearing to
  consider the following:

  A.  The Public Works Maintenance and Improvement District No. 1 - Zone A includes the
  downtown area only and was established to provide a source of funding to operate
  and maintain specialized improvements. Those improvements include items such as
  decorative sidewalk planters, landscape medians, decorative sidewalk and paving and
  the Washington Twin streetlights. This assessment is proposed to be unchanged from
  the 2025-26 level; and,

  B.  The Public Works Maintenance and Improvement District No. 1 - Zone B was
  established to fund debt service on a bond issue and ongoing maintenance and
  operation of the City’s streetlights, sidewalks, curb and gutters, streets, street trees,
  median landscaping and municipal parking lots and structures. The work is performed
  by a combination of a concrete crew, a two-person electrical crew (who also maintain
  traffic signals), an asphalt crew, and contractors. This assessment is proposed to be
  unchanged from the 2025-26 level; and,

  C.  The Public Works Maintenance and Improvement District No. 1 - Zone C was
  established in 1987 and includes generally those properties located on both sides of
  Main Street, between Atlantic and Palm, and on both sides of Palm, between Main and
  Commonwealth. The purpose of Zone C is to provide funding for the ongoing
  maintenance and operation of the public improvements, which were constructed in the
  Auto Row area and include the grass parkway, the feature lights between Atlantic and
  Olive, and the street trees. This assessment is proposed to be unchanged from the
  2025-26 level.

  Opened & Closed the Public Hearing: Mayor MALONEY opened the public hearing and as
  there was no one present who wished to speak, closed the same.

  Discussion:  Vice Mayor ANDRADE-STADLER motioned to approve the
  5
5-11-26
   resolution. Councilmember WANG and City Attorney MONTES discussed the process to
  increase fee rates. Mr. AHLEN provided further clarification regarding the current funding
  level. Ms. WANG supported the resolution, and suggested that the City could reconsider
  increasing the fees in time. Mayor MALONEY supported a future review of the rates.

  Action Taken:  City Council adopted Resolution No. R2M26-13 entitled: A
  Resolution of the Alhambra City Council ordering the renewal of the City of Alhambra
  Public Works Maintenance and Improvements District No. 1 for Fiscal Year 2026-2027
  confirming the Assessment Diagram and Assessment therefor and providing for the
  Assessment Levy in connection therewith renewing the Public Works Maintenance and
  Improvement District for the 2026-2027 Fiscal year at the same rates since 1996-97; and,
  directed staff to undertake the steps necessary to finalize Council’s action.

  Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded:  WANG
  Ayes:  ANDRADE-STADLER, LEE, MAZA, WANG, MALONEY
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

4.  PUBLIC HEARING FOR THE COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT BLOCK GRANT (CDBG)
  AND HOME PROGRAMS 2026-2027 ANNUAL ACTION PLAN) – F2M26-30, N2M26-
  35, M2M26-70

  Management Analyst ALVAREZ delivered a staff report. This was the time and place set
  by Notice No. N2M26-35 for the City Council to hold a public hearing regarding Community
  Development Block Grant (CDBG) and HOME funding for the City of Alhambra’s proposed
  2026-2027 Annual Action Plan to receive comment pursuant to and in compliance with the
  Federal Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) pre-submission
  requirements as outlined in Section 24 Part 91 of the Code of Federal Regulations.

  The City adopts a one-year Action Plan that outlines specific program activities and
  funding allocations for the upcoming program year using CDBG and HOME funds, in
  accordance with HUD requirements. The Action Plan is developed in alignment with the
  City’s five-year Consolidated Plan that was adopted in FY 2025-2026. HUD has officially
  notified the City of its funding allocations for FY 2026-2027. The City of Alhambra would
  receive approximately $823,981 in CDBG funds, an increase of $8,181 from prior year,
  and $395,699.04 in HOME funds, a decrease of $8,584.28 from prior year’s allocation.
  The Proposed Work Program for CDBG funds for FY 2026-2027 were presented in two
  alternative schedules based on the approval status of a Section 108 Loan to assist in
  building the community center: Under Schedule A, the City anticipated the approval of a
  Section 108 Loan, which would result in the allocation of $318,000.00 toward the first-year
  loan repayment obligation. As a result, funding available for direct program activities was
  adjusted accordingly. Under Schedule B, if the Section 108 Loan was not approved, no
  debt service payment would be required. As a result, the funding originally designated for
  loan repayment was reallocated to Housing Rehabilitation and Code Enforcement. The
  use of Schedule B would not constitute a substantial amendment to the Annual Action
  Plan. The complete breakdown of funding allocations for the Proposed Work Program
  (CDBG) Schedule A, Proposed Work Program (CDBG) Schedule B, and Proposed Work
  Program (HOME) were outlined in the May 11, 2026 staff report by the Assistant City
  Manager and Management Analyst.
  As part of the citizen participation process for the Annual Action Plan, the City conducted
  two interactive pre-planning sessions with the HCDA Citizen Advisory Committee on
  6
5-11-26
   February 3, 2026, and April 7, 2026. These sessions focused on identifying funding
  priorities and developing program recommendations. To ensure broad community input,
  the City extended invitations to 110 community organizations serving low- and moderate-
  income populations, as well as to neighboring jurisdictions to the April 7, 2026 meeting.
  The HCDA Citizen Advisory Committee reviewed the draft Annual Action Plan on May 5,
  2026, and unanimously recommended it be approved by Council.

  Open Public Hearing:  Mayor Maloney opened the public hearing.

  Public Comment:  Lewis McCammon discussed the process for the Annual
  Action Plan and the role of the HCDA Citizen Advisory Committee.

  Close Public Hearing:  After receiving public comment, Mayor Maloney closed the
  public hearing.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Take:  City Council approved the proposed FY 2026- 2027 Annual Action
  Plan for the Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) and HOME Investment
  Partnerships programs, and authorized staff to submit these plans to the U.S. Department
  of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). (M2M26-70)

  Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded:  WANG
  Ayes:  MAZA, WANG, ANDRADE-STADLER, LEE, MALONEY
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

PRESENTATIONS

5.  AMENDED BUDGET REVIEW AND RESOLUTION ADOPTING FY 2026-27 BUDGET
  ADJUSTMENTS – F2M25-17, R2M26-12

  Director of Finance LIEU delivered the presentation and staff report. On June 23, 2025,
  the City Council adopted the Fiscal Years 2025-26 and 2026-27 Budget. On February 23,
  2026, the Mid-Year Budget Review was presented, and the City Council approved the
  recommended budget adjustments for Fiscal Year 2025-26. Since then, staff has
  continued to monitor revenues and expenditures and is now presenting the Amended
  Budget Review to update the City’s financial projections and appropriations for Fiscal Year
  2026-27. Fiscal Year 2025-26 ended with an unappropriated surplus of $2,007,354,
  primarily attributable to higher-than-anticipated revenues. These increases were driven by
  stronger-than-projected property tax receipts resulting from rising assessed values, CPI
  adjustments, and property reassessments, as well as growth in service charges, grant
  reimbursements, and interest earnings. These gains were partially offset by declines in
  sales tax revenues and transfers supporting capital improvement projects. For Fiscal Year
  2026-27, staff presents an Amended General Fund Budget reflecting a projected deficit of
  $1,482,209. When combined with the Fiscal Year 2025-26 surplus, the overall
  unappropriated surplus is $525,145. Historically, such surpluses have been allocated to
  priority needs, including reserve contributions, capital repair and replacement, pension
  and retirement obligations, and the acquisition of essential equipment. Appropriations to
  these efforts are made through City Council-approved budget adjustments. City Manager
  BINNQUIST requested Council review the 2026 Strategic Plan Funding
  Recommendations and provide direction to staff.
  7
5-11-26
   Discussion:  Council provided funding recommendations for 2026 Strategic Plan
  goals and how to allocate monies from the $525,145.00 surplus. Council had a robust
  discussion and reached consensus to allocate funds for the following: expand the CERT
  Program for $500,000.00, upgrade Gateway Plaza, including a landscape plan, for
  $10,000.00, add funds to Sidewalk Repairs for $150,000.00, add funds to the
  Sustainability Plan projects for $160,145.00, and add $200,00.00 to the Reserves fund.
  City Manager BINNQUIST provided clarification during the discussion as needed.

  In their discussion, Council noted the other unfunded Strategic Plan Goals and discussed
  their importance. Council directed staff to continue to seek additional funding sources. Ms.
  BINNQUIST stated that staff would update Council at the mid-year point and would
  continue seeking grants and not move forward with General Fund money. Ms. LIEU then
  continued her budget presentation.

  Action Taken:  City Council received and filed the Amended Budget Review for
  Fiscal Year 2026-27 and related reports; and, adopted Resolution No. R2M26-12
  entitled: A Resolution of the Alhambra City Council adopting Fiscal Years 2025-26 and
  2026-27 Budget adjustments of the City of Alhambra, Golf Course Clubhouse Corporation,
  Alhambra Capital Improvements Corporation, Alhambra Parking Authority, Alhambra
  Facilities Financing Authority and the Alhambra Public Financing Authority approving the
  Fiscal Year 2026-27 budget adjustments.

  Vote:  Moved:  MAZA  Seconded:  ANDRADE-STADLER
  Ayes:  LEE, ANDRADE-STADLER, WANG, MAZA, MALONEY
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

CONSENT AGENDA (Item Nos. 6 – 22): (TIME LIMITATIONS: 5 MINUTES PER SPEAKER
FOR ONE ITEM, 10 MINUTES PER SPEAKER FOR 2+ ITEMS)

All items listed under the Consent Agenda, with the exception of Item Nos. 10, 17, 20, 21, and 22,
were considered by the City Council to be routine and were enacted by one motion.

6.  AWARD CONTRACT: PURCHASE OF CARBON MEDIA FOR THE GROUND WATER
  TREATMENT PLANT – F2M26-6B, RFP2M26-3, C2M26-26, M2M26-69

  On March 23, 2026, the City Council approved distribution of a Request for Proposals for
  the purchase of carbon filter media for the Ground Water Treatment Plant. On April 23,
  2026, two proposals were received. Staff conducted a review and evaluation of the
  responding proposals and Calgon Carbon Corporation was selected based on their
  qualifications, standards of quality, capability to deliver product throughout the contract
  term, third party hauling company’s reputation, flexibility, references and cost of the
  product. Additionally, Calgon Carbon Corporation provides carbon that is approved by the
  State of California State Water Resources Control Board - Division of Drinking Water to
  be used at the City’s Ground Water Treatment Plant.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council awarded a contract, subject to final language approval
  by the City Manager and City Attorney, by and between the City of Alhambra and the
  Calgon Carbon Corporation for the purchase and installation of carbon filter media at the
  8
5-11-26
   Ground Water Treatment Plant in an amount not to exceed $350,000.00 for one year, with
  two additional two-year renewal options, for a total amount not to exceed $1,050,000.00
  over a three-year period, authorized the City Manager to execute the extensions if the
  services are satisfactory; and directed staff to undertake the steps necessary to finalize
  Council's action. (M2M26-69)

  Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded:  LEE
  Ayes:  LEE, ANDRADE-STADLER, WANG, MAZA, MALONEY
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

7.  AWARD CONTRACT: PROFESSIONAL ENGINEERING DESIGN SERVICES FOR
  PRIORITY PEDESTRIAN IMPROVEMENTS PROJECT – F2M25-62, RFP2M25-26,
  C2M26-27, M2M26-71

  On March 11, 2024, the City Council adopted the City’s Bicycle and Pedestrian
  Improvement Plan (“Walk, Bike, Move Alhambra!”), which established a vision for biking
  and pedestrian infrastructure and facilitates further planning and funding support for the
  implementation of the City’s multi-modal transportation goals. The City received a Funding
  Agreement in the amount of $14,387,027.50 in Measure R funds for the Citywide Priority
  Pedestrian Improvement Project on October 6, 2025. The funding would cover the design,
  engineering, and construction associated with improving the eight priority pedestrian
  locations identified in the City’s Bicycle and Pedestrian Improvement Plan. On December
  8, 2025, staff obtained authorization to distribute the Request for Proposals for design
  engineering services for priority pedestrian improvements. The design engineering service
  would cover the Project’s Phase 1 PS&E and Phase 2 Preliminary Engineering. Staff
  received and reviewed four proposals. AYCE Consulting Engineers, Inc. was selected
  based on their technical approach, project team qualifications, relevant experience,
  references, and completeness and quality of the proposal.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council awarded a contract to AYCE Consulting Engineers,
  Inc., subject to final language approval by the City Manager and City Attorney, in the
  amount of $878,325.22 for professional engineering design services for the City’s Priority
  Pedestrian Improvements under the Alhambra Bicycle and Pedestrian Improvement Plan,
  and directed staff to undertake the steps necessary to finalize the Council’s action.
  (M2M26-71)

  Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded:  LEE
  Ayes:  LEE, ANDRADE-STADLER, WANG, MAZA, MALONEY
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

8.  LETTER OF SUPPORT FOR THE COALITION TO PROTECT COMMUNITY SERVICES
  – F2M26-19, M2M26-72

  On May 4, 2026, the California Joint Power Insurance Authority (CJPIA), reached out to
  the City requesting support for a new legislative advocacy effort, led by the CJPIA - the
  Coalition to Protect Community Services. Since 2018, the City has been a member of
  CJPIA, one of the largest municipal self-insurance pools in the state of California, with
  more than 125 member cities and public agencies. In recent years, the liability
  9
5-11-26
   environment for local agencies has become increasingly challenging, with costs rising
  sharply due to higher claim severity, a more complex litigation landscape, and broader
  systematic factors affecting CJPIA member agencies and public agencies throughout the
  state. Rising liability costs are directly impacting local budgets and essential community
  services, which is why CJPIA sought support for this new legislative advocacy effort. The
  Coalition would bring cities, counties, schools, special districts and other local agencies
  together to advocate for a more balanced and sustainable liability environment though
  targeted reforms to state law. Per CJPIA, the effort is focused on protecting public
  resources while ensuring fair compensation for people injured by local government
  negligence.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council approved the letter of support for the Coalition to
  Protect Community Services as outlined in the May 11, 2026 staff report by the Director
  of Human Resources and Risk Management; and, directed staff to undertake the steps
  necessary to finalize the City Council’s action. (M2M26-72)

  Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded:  LEE
  Ayes:  LEE, ANDRADE-STADLER, WANG, MAZA, MALONEY
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

9.  APPROVAL OF CONTRACT WITH THE ALHAMBRA CENTRAL BUSINESS DISTRICT
  ASSOCIATION (ACBDA) FOR FISCAL YEAR 2026-2027 – F2M21-50, C2M26-28,
  M2M26-73

  Since 1974, the City has maintained an agreement with the ACBDA to provide promotional
  support to the merchants in the Alhambra Central Business District of Association. These
  merchants are assessed in accordance with the Alhambra Municipal Code Section
  5.04.201. The City collects the assessment and allocates it for marketing and promotion
  activities specific to the Business District area. According to the City’s agreement with the
  ACBDA, a maximum of ninety percent (90%) of the total funds collected each year by the
  City may be allocated to the ACBDA. The Fiscal Year 2026- 2027 minimum allocation total
  was estimated to be $85,500. In previous years, the estimated minimum has been
  exceeded This year, ACBDA requested a $80,000 advance on the agreement. The
  proposed work plan for 2026-2027 was attached with a focus on branding,
  events//programing, business support and engagement.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council awarded a contract to the Alhambra Central Business
  District Association (ACBDA), subject to final language approval by the City Manager and
  City Attorney, for the promotion of the Central Business District for the 2026-2027 Fiscal
  Year; and, directed staff to undertake the steps necessary to finalize the Council’s action.
  (M2M26-73)

  Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded:  LEE
  Ayes:  LEE, ANDRADE-STADLER, WANG, MAZA, MALONEY
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

 10.  AGREEMENT TO LEASE A PORTION OF THE CITY OF ALHAMBRA’S RAYMOND
  BASIN WATER RIGHTS TO THE HUNTINGTON LIBRARY – F2M9-62, M2M26-74

  The City owns 1031 acre-feet of water rights in the Raymond Basin for Fiscal Year 2025-
  26. Respectively, the City pays $36,304.00 in assessment fees (annually) for water rights

20.  CONSIDERATION OF AN ORDINANCE ADDING SECTION 3.12.180 (TWO YEAR

  2.34.020(C), 9.12.030 AND 19.01.010(SEC. 102)(G) OF THE ALHAMBRA MUNICIPAL
  CODE PERTAINING TO THE QUALIFICATIONS FOR MEMBERS OF THE PLANNING
  COMMISSION, PARKS & RECREATION COMMISSION, LIBRARY BOARD AND
  TRANSPORTATION COMMISSION AS WELL AS DAYTIME LOITERING AND THE
  SALE OF SAFE AND SANE FIREWORKS – F2M26-16, O2M26-4862

  The Alhambra Municipal Code (“AMC”) is a comprehensive gathering of ordinances
  adopted by the City Council covering a wide range of topics. From time-to-time updates
  are made to the AMC to address new state legislation, clarify ambiguous provisions, or
  delete outdated language. While some of these changes require immediate consideration
  by the Council, most can be addressed periodically. For this annual review, City staff
  suggested minor changes to the AMC to reflect current practices and clarify confusing
  parts of the AMC. First, City staff identified the proposed addition of Section 3.12.180 (Two
  Year Budget) which would allow for the preparation of two-year budgets, which has been
  staff’s and the Council’s recent practice and preference to better stabilize the City’s
  finances. Staff also identified proposed amendments to Sections 2.24.020, 2.28.020,
  2.32.030, 2.34.020 (Qualifications – Parks & Recreation Commission, Board of Library
  Trustees and Transportation Commission) which would further clarify the residency
  requirements for members of those Boards/Commissions. Furthermore, staff proposed
  amendments to Section 9.12.030 (Loitering; Daytime) which would change the truancy
  hours from 8:30 a.m. to 1:30 p.m. daily to instead refer to “school hours,” given the
  variation in school hours on a daily basis, and by school. A minor stopped for a potential
  violation would only be cited if the particular school they attend was in session at that time
  and the minor was not excused from attendance. Finally, staff proposed an amendment
  to Section 19.01.010 (Sale of Safe and Sane Fireworks) to address an inconsistency
  between the fee amount currently stated in the City’s adopted ordinance as it pertained to
  the sales of Safe and Sane fireworks and the City’s adopted Master Fee Schedule. To
  ensure accuracy and flexibility moving forward, the proposed ordinance would remove the
  specific fee amount and instead direct the public to the City’s current fee schedule, as
  adopted and periodically updated by resolution of the City Council.

  and Commissions as well as the other changes to AMC.

22.  SECOND READING AND ADOPTION OF AN ORDINANCE ADDING CHAPTER 6.29
  (“RESIDENTIAL TENANT PROTECTIONS”) TO TITLE VI (HEALTH AND
  SANITATION) OF THE ALHAMBRA MUNICIPAL CODE ESTABLISHING AN
  INCREASED RELOCATION ASSISTANCE OBLIGATION ON CERTAIN NO-FAULT
  RESIDENTIAL EVICTIONS IN THE CITY OF ALHAMBRA – F2M26-7, O2M26-4861

  Staff is requesting that the City Council consider second reading and adoption of an
  ordinance adding Chapter 6.29 (Residential Tenant Protections) To Title VI (Health and
  Sanitation) of the Alhambra Municipal Code establishing an increased relocation
  assistance obligation on certain no-fault residential evictions in the City of Alhambra. On
  April 13, 2026, the City Council directed staff to prepare an ordinance to increase
  relocation assistance payments for no-fault evictions from one (1) month to three (3)
  months’ rent. The proposed ordinance would add Chapter 6.29 to the City’s Municipal
  Code, requiring that in those circumstances where relocation assistance is required under
  AB 1482, that the obligation would be increased from one to three months. To the extent
  that an owner/landlord does not comply with this requirement, the ordinance provides that
  such noncompliance can be asserted as a defense in any action brought by the owner to
  recover possession of a residential unit. Under AB 1482, landlords are required to provide
  relocation assistance for certain no-fault evictions, including owner move-in, substantial
  rehabilitation, demolition, or withdrawal of units from the rental market. The proposed
  ordinance was given first reading at the April 27, 2026 City Council meeting.

  Public Comment:
  The following people spoke against the proposed ordinance:
  1) Adam Bray-Ali
  2) Lorraine Clack
  3) Charles Stapleton and Jose Ortiz
  4) Joseph Ramos
  5) Nanette Ong
  6) Danny Sam
  7) Mindy Ye, speaking on behalf of Becky Chan

  The following people spoke in favor of the proposed ordinance:
  8) Lewis McCammon

  Discussion:  Councilmember WANG and City Attorney MONTES discussed the
  ways the ordinance related to AB 1482. Mr. MONTES provided further clarification
  regarding the ordinance. Ms. WANG continued to address public concerns. She supported
  tenant relocation assistance, but stated that she would be open to additional

  18
5-11-26
   considerations to “mom and pop” landlords to mitigate the potential impacts on small
  property owners.

  Councilmember MAZA expressed sympathy with the speakers as a property owner and
  realtor. He went on to discuss the recent case at 110 S. Chapel Ave and the need to
  support evicted people. He agreed with Ms. Wang’s suggestion to consider language to
  mitigate impact on small property owners. He suggested carving out 1-4 units, to include
  a section which would state that the 3 months relocation would apply in cases where the
  eviction is due to demolition or substantial remodel. He also requested staff return with
  more information regarding monitoring the ordinance.

  Mayor MALONEY spoke to Council’s intent for the ordinance and spoke to the challenges
  to balance protecting tenants from landlords and protecting landlords with good intention.
  Council continued to discuss SB 552 and guidelines for renovation as well as past cases
  where landlords have displaced tenants. Council discussed the need to prevent
  homelessness. Vice Mayor ANDRADE-STADLER supported the exception for 1-4 units
  and suggested more regulation for corporate owners.

  Councilmember LEE and Mr. MONTES further discussed the exceptions provided in the
  proposed ordinance. Ms. LEE did not support further exception for 1-4 units and continued
  to support the ordinance as written. She stated that she could support exception for 1-2
  units. Mr. MONTES provided further clarification as to the application of the ordinance.

  Mr. MAZA motioned to move forward with the existing ordinance, with amendments for
  eviction related to demolition and to exclude 1-4 units from the ordinance. Ms. ANDRADE-
  STADLER seconded the motion. Ms. LEE proposed a substitute motion for exceptions for
  single family homes and duplexes, which did not receive a second. Ms. Lee’s motion
  failed.

  Council continued to discuss the ordinance and the proposed exemption for 1-4 units. Mr.
  MONTES provided additional clarification and stated that due to the number of proposed
  changes, staff would have to bring the ordinance back revised for a first reading. Mr.
  MALONEY clarified Council direction to amend the ordinance to create a new exemption
  for properties of 4 units or under, except in cases where the property is being demolition
  or substantial renovation then the 3 month assistance would apply. Mr. MONTES and
  Council discussed where in cases where the 3 months assistance would still apply under
  the ordinance. Mr. MAZA suggested Council review the ordinance after a year.

  Action Taken:  Council directed staff to return with revisions made to the ordinance
  for a first reading at the next City Council meeting.
